# Overview



TorchSim is a next-generation atomistic simulation engine built entirely in PyTorch, designed from the ground up to unlock massive performance gains for machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). By rewriting the fundamental primitives of atomistic simulation — state management, force computation, integration, and optimization — as differentiable PyTorch operations, TorchSim achieves up to **100× speedup** over traditional Python-based frameworks like ASE while maintaining a familiar, beginner-friendly API.

![Speedup comparison](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TorchSim/torch-sim/main/docs/_static/speedup_plot.svg)

This speedup comes from three architectural pillars: **native GPU execution**, **automatic batching** of multiple independent simulations, and **efficient GPU memory management**. Where ASE processes one system at a time on the CPU, TorchSim can run dozens or even hundreds of systems simultaneously on a single GPU, filling available memory to maximize throughput.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L30)

## Why TorchSim?

Traditional atomistic simulation frameworks were designed for classical force fields running on CPUs. They process one structure at a time, leaving GPU resources underutilized. MLIPs, which are neural network models, are inherently GPU-friendly — but the surrounding simulation infrastructure (integrators, optimizers, neighbor lists, state management) remained CPU-bound, creating a bottleneck. TorchSim eliminates this bottleneck by implementing the entire simulation loop in PyTorch, enabling end-to-end GPU acceleration and unlocking the ability to process many systems in parallel through batching.

The following table summarizes how TorchSim compares to a traditional Python-based simulation workflow:

| Feature | Traditional (ASE) | TorchSim |
|---|---|---|
| Execution device | CPU only | CPU or GPU (CUDA) |
| Simulation parallelism | Sequential (one system at a time) | **Batched** (many systems simultaneously) |
| Memory management | Manual | **Automatic** (adaptive batching) |
| Force models | Classical + MLIP wrappers | Native MLIP adapters + classical potentials |
| Differentiability | Limited | **Fully differentiable** through PyTorch |
| Trajectory format | ASE `.traj` (pickle) | **HDF5-based** binary with compression |
| Unit system | Various | Metal units (Å, eV, amu, ps) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L15), [torch_sim/units.py](torch_sim/units.py#L84-L103)

## Architecture at a Glance

TorchSim follows a modular, functional architecture where every simulation method (integrator, optimizer, Monte Carlo propagator) is decomposed into an `init` function and a `step` function. The `init` function creates a specialized state object, and the `step` function advances that state by one iteration. This design enables maximum flexibility: you can use the high-level runners for common workflows, or compose your own simulation loops from the low-level building blocks.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "User API Layer"
        A["ts.integrate()"]
        B["ts.optimize()"]
        C["ts.static()"]
```

This diagram shows the layered architecture of TorchSim. At the top, high-level runners (`integrate`, `optimize`, `static`) provide a simple entry point. These delegate to the state and simulation engine layers, which in turn depend on models and shared infrastructure. The interoperability layer connects TorchSim to the broader Python materials science ecosystem.

Sources: [torch_sim/__init__.py](torch_sim/__init__.py#L1-L80), [torch_sim/runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L1-L10)

## Core Concepts

TorchSim is organized around five core concepts that every user should understand. Each concept is explored in depth in dedicated tutorial notebooks, but here we provide a concise overview of how they fit together.

### SimState — The Heart of Everything

`SimState` is the central data structure in TorchSim. It represents one or more atomistic systems as PyTorch tensors, holding positions, masses, cell matrices, atomic numbers, and periodic boundary conditions. What makes `SimState` powerful is its native support for **batching**: a single `SimState` can represent dozens of independent systems simultaneously, with a `system_idx` tensor mapping each atom to its parent system.

![TorchSim package treemap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TorchSim/torch-sim/main/docs/_static/torch-sim-pkg-treemap.svg)

`SimState` supports slicing (`state[[0, 2, 4]]`), cloning, splitting into individual systems, and conversion to ASE `Atoms`, Pymatgen `Structure`, or Phonopy `PhonopyAtoms` objects. All tensor attributes live on the same device, making device transfers a single `.to(device)` call away.

Sources: [torch_sim/state.py](torch_sim/state.py#L70-L125)

### Runners — Your High-Level API

The three runner functions provide a unified, high-level interface for the most common simulation tasks:

| Runner | Purpose | Key Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `ts.integrate()` | Run molecular dynamics | `integrator`, `n_steps`, `temperature`, `timestep` |
| `ts.optimize()` | Relax atomic positions (and cell) | `optimizer`, `convergence_fn`, `max_steps` |
| `ts.static()` | Single-point energy/force evaluation | (none beyond `system` and `model`) |

All runners accept an ASE `Atoms`, Pymatgen `Structure`, or an existing `SimState` as input. They share a common pattern: you provide a system, a model, and method-specific parameters, and you get back an optimized or evolved state. Autobatching and trajectory reporting can be enabled with simple flags or configuration dictionaries.

Sources: [torch_sim/runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L252-L265), [torch_sim/runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L551-L565), [torch_sim/runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L734-L742)

### Models — Pluggable Force Fields

TorchSim provides a uniform `ModelInterface` that all models implement. This abstract base class, extending `torch.nn.Module`, requires a `forward()` method that takes a `SimState` and returns a dictionary with at minimum `energy` and `forces` (and optionally `stress`). This means switching between models requires changing only the model object — the rest of your simulation code stays identical.

The following MLIP models are supported out of the box:

| Model | Package | Install Extra |
|---|---|---|
| MACE / MACE-MPA | `mace-torch` | `torch-sim[mace]` |
| FairChem (OC20/OC22) | `fairchem-core` | `torch-sim[fairchem]` |
| SevenNet | `sevenn` | `torch-sim[sevenn]` |
| MatterSim | `mattersim` | `torch-sim[mattersim]` |
| ORB | `orb-models` | `torch-sim[orb]` |
| Graph-PES (PET/PET-MAD) | `graph-pes` + `mace-torch` | `torch-sim[graphpes]` |
| Metatomic | `metatomic-torch` | `torch-sim[metatomic]` |
| NequIP | `nequip` | `torch-sim[nequip]` |

Classical potentials — Lennard-Jones, Morse, and soft-sphere — are also included and require no additional dependencies.

> [!TIP]
> All runners use the **metal unit system** (Å for distance, eV for energy, amu for mass, ps for time) internally. When passing temperatures to `integrate()`, convert from Kelvin using `ts.units.temperature` (approximately 8.617e-5 eV/K), or let the runner handle the conversion for you.

Sources: [torch_sim/models/interface.py](torch_sim/models/interface.py#L38-L136), [torch_sim/integrators/__init__.py](torch_sim/integrators/__init__.py#L8-L25), [torch_sim/units.py](torch_sim/units.py#L84-L103)

### Integrators and Optimizers

TorchSim implements a comprehensive set of molecular dynamics integrators and geometry optimizers, each following the `init`/`step` pattern and fully compatible with batched states.

**Integrators** for molecular dynamics:

| Integrator | Ensemble | Thermostat / Barostat |
|---|---|---|
| `ts.Integrator.nve` | Microcanonical | None (constant energy) |
| `ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin` | Canonical | BAOAB Langevin |
| `ts.Integrator.nvt_vrescale` | Canonical | Velocity rescaling (Bussi) |
| `ts.Integrator.nvt_nose_hoover` | Canonical | Nosé-Hoover chain |
| `ts.Integrator.npt_langevin` | Isothermal-isobaric | Langevin thermostat + Langevin barostat |
| `ts.Integrator.npt_nose_hoover` | Isothermal-isobaric | Nosé-Hoover chain |
| `ts.Integrator.npt_isotropic_crescale` | Isothermal-isobaric | C-Rescale (isotropic) |
| `ts.Integrator.npt_anisotropic_crescale` | Isothermal-isobaric | C-Rescale (anisotropic) |

**Optimizers** for geometry relaxation:

| Optimizer | Type | Best For |
|---|---|---|
| `ts.Optimizer.gradient_descent` | First-order | Simple debugging, educational use |
| `ts.Optimizer.fire` | First-order | Robust relaxation of atoms and cell |
| `ts.Optimizer.lbfgs` | Quasi-Newton | Fast convergence, memory-efficient |
| `ts.Optimizer.bfgs` | Quasi-Newton | Fast convergence with full Hessian approx. |

Cell optimization during relaxation is handled by **cell filters** such as `ts.CellFilter.frechet`, which parameterizes the cell deformation space to maintain physical constraints.

Sources: [torch_sim/integrators/__init__.py](torch_sim/integrators/__init__.py#L97-L131), [torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py](torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py#L38-L44)

### Autobatching — Maximizing GPU Utilization

One of TorchSim's most distinctive features is its automatic batching system. Different MLIP models consume GPU memory at different rates, and memory usage scales differently depending on the neighbor list algorithm. Manually tuning batch sizes is tedious and error-prone. TorchSim solves this with two complementary strategies:

- **`BinningAutoBatcher`**: Groups systems into fixed bins that fit in GPU memory. Ideal when you have all systems available upfront (e.g., a dataset of candidate structures to relax).
- **`InFlightAutoBatcher`**: Dynamically adds and removes systems from the current batch as they complete. Ideal when systems converge at different rates (e.g., optimizing structures with varying difficulty).

Simply pass `autobatcher=True` to `integrate()` or `optimize()`, and TorchSim will automatically measure GPU memory, determine the optimal batch size, and process systems in memory-safe chunks.

Sources: [torch_sim/autobatching.py](torch_sim/autobatching.py#L520-L574), [torch_sim/autobatching.py](torch_sim/autobatching.py#L813-L878)

## Package Structure

The `torch_sim` package is organized into focused submodules, each responsible for a clear domain of functionality:

```
torch_sim/
├── state.py              # SimState and state utilities
├── runners.py            # High-level integrate/optimize/static API
├── models/               # MLIP and classical model adapters
│   ├── interface.py      # Abstract ModelInterface
│   ├── mace.py           # MACE adapter
│   ├── fairchem.py       # FairChem adapter
│   ├── sevennet.py       # SevenNet adapter
│   ├── mattersim.py      # MatterSim adapter
│   ├── orb.py            # ORB adapter
│   ├── graphpes.py       # Graph-PES adapter
│   ├── metatomic.py      # Metatomic adapter
│   ├── lennard_jones.py  # Classical LJ potential
│   ├── morse.py          # Classical Morse potential
│   └── soft_sphere.py    # Classical soft-sphere potential
├── integrators/          # MD integration schemes
│   ├── md.py             # Base MD state and step logic
│   ├── nve.py            # Velocity Verlet (NVE)
│   ├── nvt.py            # NVT thermostats (Langevin, V-Rescale, NH)
│   └── npt.py            # NPT barostats (Langevin, NH, C-Rescale)
├── optimizers/           # Geometry optimization algorithms
│   ├── gradient_descent.py
│   ├── fire.py
│   ├── lbfgs.py
│   ├── bfgs.py
│   └── cell_filters.py   # Cell parameterization (Frechet, etc.)
├── autobatching.py       # BinningAutoBatcher, InFlightAutoBatcher
├── neighbors/            # Neighbor list backends
│   ├── vesin.py          # Vesin (high-performance, optional)
│   ├── torch_nl.py       # Pure PyTorch neighbor lists
│   └── alchemiops.py     # AlchemiOps integration
├── trajectory.py         # HDF5 trajectory I/O (TorchSimTrajectory, TrajectoryReporter)
├── constraints.py        # FixAtoms, FixCom, FixSymmetry
├── transforms.py         # PBC wrapping, coordinate transforms, linked-cell algorithm
├── monte_carlo.py        # Swap Monte Carlo (Metropolis criterion)
├── elastic.py            # Elastic tensor calculation
├── workflows/            # Higher-level workflows (amorphous-to-crystalline)
├── io.py                 # ASE / Pymatgen / Phonopy conversion
├── units.py              # Metal and Real unit systems
├── quantities.py         # Thermodynamic quantities (KE, temperature, pressure)
├── properties/           # Correlation functions (RDF, S(q))
└── symmetrize.py         # Symmetry analysis utilities
```

Sources: [torch_sim/__init__.py](torch_sim/__init__.py#L1-L80)

## Beyond the Basics

In addition to core molecular dynamics and geometry optimization, TorchSim offers several advanced capabilities that make it a comprehensive platform for computational materials science:

- **Constraints**: Fix specific atoms (`FixAtoms`), remove center-of-mass motion (`FixCom`), or preserve crystal symmetry during relaxation (`FixSymmetry`). All constraints integrate seamlessly with integrators and optimizers in batched mode.
- **Swap Monte Carlo**: Perform atomic species swaps using the Metropolis criterion, enabling solid-state mixing and alloy sampling. Works with the `integrate()` runner and supports trajectory reporting.
- **Elastic Properties**: Calculate the full elastic tensor for any crystal system, with symmetry-aware strain generation and Voigt notation handling.
- **Amorphous-to-Crystalline (A2C) Workflow**: A complete workflow for generating random packed structures, performing simulated crystallization via simulated annealing, and extracting candidate crystal structures from disordered precursors.
- **Trajectory Reporting**: Write simulation trajectories to efficient HDF5 files with on-the-fly compression, supporting arbitrary user-defined properties alongside standard state data.
- **Differentiability**: Because everything is PyTorch, the entire simulation is differentiable — enabling gradient-based inverse design, force-matching, and other ML training workflows that require gradients through the simulation.

Sources: [torch_sim/constraints.py](torch_sim/constraints.py#L28-L34), [torch_sim/monte_carlo.py](torch_sim/monte_carlo.py#L36-L56), [torch_sim/elastic.py](torch_sim/elastic.py#L1-L20), [torch_sim/workflows/a2c.py](torch_sim/workflows/a2c.py#L1-L8), [torch_sim/trajectory.py](torch_sim/trajectory.py#L1-L12)

## Installation

Install TorchSim from PyPI with a single command:

```sh
pip install torch-sim-atomistic
```

Then install the extras for the MLIP models you want to use. For example, to use MACE:

```sh
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mace]
```

For full interoperability with ASE, Pymatgen, and Phonopy:

```sh
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[io]
```

You can install from source if you want to contribute or use the latest development version:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/TorchSim/torch-sim
cd torch-sim
pip install .
```

TorchSim requires **Python 3.12+** and **PyTorch 2+**.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L99-L112), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L33-L60)

# Quick Start



This guide walks you through your first TorchSim simulation in under five minutes. You will run a molecular dynamics simulation, perform a geometry optimization, and process multiple systems in parallel — all using TorchSim's high-level API. By the end, you will understand the three core runner functions (`integrate`, `optimize`, `static`), the `SimState` data model, and how TorchSim unifies ASE and PyMatGen inputs under a single GPU-accelerated interface.

## How TorchSim Works

TorchSim is a PyTorch-native atomistic simulation library. Unlike traditional MD packages that process one structure at a time on a CPU, TorchSim batches multiple atomic systems into unified tensors and executes them on GPU hardware. This architectural decision yields significant throughput improvements, especially for machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) that are already implemented in PyTorch.

The library follows a layered design. At the bottom, `SimState` represents atomic systems as flat tensors with a `system_idx` mapping. Models implement a `ModelInterface` that accepts `SimState` and returns energy, forces, and stress. Above that, low-level integrators and optimizers expose `init_fn`/`step_fn` pairs. At the top, three high-level runner functions — `integrate`, `optimize`, and `static` — orchestrate the full simulation lifecycle including state initialization, trajectory reporting, and automatic batching.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Inputs["Input Formats"]
        ASE["ASE Atoms"]
        PMG["PyMatGen Structure"]
        SS["SimState"]
    end

    subgraph Core["Core Layer"]
        IS["initialize_state()"]
        STATE["SimState<br/>positions, masses, cell,<br/>atomic_numbers, system_idx"]
        MODEL["ModelInterface<br/>(LennardJones, MACE, MACE-MPA,<br/>SevenNet, ORB, FairChem, ...)"]
    end

    subgraph Runners["High-Level Runners"]
        INT["integrate()<br/>Molecular Dynamics"]
        OPT["optimize()<br/>Geometry Optimization"]
        STA["static()<br/>Single-Point Calc"]
    end

    subgraph Outputs["Outputs"]
        TA["ASE Atoms"]
        TR["TrajectoryReporter<br/>(HDF5 files)"]
        RES["Property Dictionaries"]
    end

    ASE --> IS
    PMG --> IS
    SS --> IS
    IS --> STATE
    STATE --> MODEL
    STATE --> INT
    MODEL --> INT
    STATE --> OPT
    MODEL --> OPT
    STATE --> STA
    MODEL --> STA
    INT --> TA
    INT --> TR
    OPT --> TA
    OPT --> TR
    STA --> RES
    STA --> TR
```

## Your First Simulation

Install TorchSim with a classical potential model to get started immediately — no GPU or external MLIP package is required for this example.

```bash
pip install torch-sim-atomistic
```

Then run a minimal NVT molecular dynamics simulation using the built-in Lennard-Jones potential. This example creates an FCC copper structure, simulates it at 2000 K for 50 steps using a Langevin thermostat, and returns the final state.

```python
import torch
import torch_sim as ts
from ase.build import bulk
from torch_sim.models.lennard_jones import LennardJonesModel

# 1. Define the atomic potential model
lj_model = LennardJonesModel(
    sigma=2.0,        # Å, interaction distance parameter
    epsilon=0.1,      # eV, interaction strength
    device=torch.device("cpu"),
    dtype=torch.float64,
)

# 2. Create an atomic structure (ASE Atoms object)
cu_atoms = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=5.43, cubic=True)

# 3. Run the simulation
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=cu_atoms,                       # Input: ASE Atoms, PyMatGen Structure, or SimState
    model=lj_model,                        # Any model implementing ModelInterface
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin, # Thermostat ensemble
    n_steps=50,                            # Number of integration steps
    temperature=2000,                      # Target temperature in Kelvin
    timestep=0.002,                        # Integration timestep in picoseconds
)

# 4. Convert back to familiar formats
final_atoms = final_state.to_atoms()        # → list of ASE Atoms
# final_structures = final_state.to_structures()  # → list of PyMatGen Structures
```

Sources: [high_level_tutorial.py](examples/tutorials/high_level_tutorial.py#L50-L82), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L252-L270), [__init__.py](torch_sim/__init__.py#L94-L100)

### What Just Happened

The `integrate` function performed several operations automatically. It called `initialize_state()` to convert the ASE Atoms object into a `SimState` with properly shaped tensors, applied the **MetalUnits** unit system internally (Å, eV, amu, ps), resolved the integrator from the `INTEGRATOR_REGISTRY` to obtain its `init_fn` and `step_fn`, then executed the time-stepping loop. The temperature and timestep values you provided in human-readable units (Kelvin, picoseconds) were converted to the internal eV-based unit system automatically by the runner.

The `SimState` dataclass is the central data structure. It holds per-atom tensors — `positions`, `masses`, `atomic_numbers`, and `system_idx` — alongside per-system tensors like `cell`. The `system_idx` tensor maps each atom to its parent system, which is how TorchSim packs multiple structures into contiguous memory for GPU execution.

Sources: [state.py](torch_sim/state.py#L70-L124), [units.py](torch_sim/units.py#L84-L104), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L310-L330)

## Saving and Analyzing Trajectories

Passing a dictionary with a `filenames` key to `trajectory_reporter` enables automatic trajectory output. TorchSim writes HDF5 files that store both the atomic state at configurable intervals and any computed properties.

```python
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=cu_atoms,
    model=lj_model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=50,
    temperature=2000,
    timestep=0.002,
    trajectory_reporter={"filenames": "cu_md_trajectory.h5"},
)

# Analyze saved data
with ts.TorchSimTrajectory("cu_md_trajectory.h5") as traj:
    potential_energies = traj.get_array("potential_energy")
    kinetic_energies = traj.get_array("kinetic_energy")
    final_config = traj.get_atoms(-1)  # ASE Atoms at last saved frame

print(f"Final energy: {potential_energies[-1].item():.6f} eV")
```

For finer control over what gets saved and how often, instantiate a `TrajectoryReporter` directly. You can specify per-property reporting frequencies, which is useful for quantities like kinetic energy that you may want to sample less frequently than the state itself.

Sources: [high_level_tutorial.py](examples/tutorials/high_level_tutorial.py#L94-L155), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L258-L262)

## Geometry Optimization

The `optimize` function relaxes atomic structures using algorithms like FIRE or L-BFGS. It accepts a `convergence_fn` that returns a boolean tensor indicating which systems have converged. If you omit this argument, TorchSim applies a default energy convergence criterion of 1 meV between successive steps.

```python
final_state = ts.optimize(
    system=cu_atoms,
    model=lj_model,
    optimizer=ts.Optimizer.fire,
    init_kwargs={"cell_filter": ts.CellFilter.unit},  # Allow unit cell relaxation
)

# With custom convergence criteria
force_convergence = ts.generate_force_convergence_fn(force_tol=1e-3)
final_state = ts.optimize(
    system=cu_atoms,
    model=lj_model,
    optimizer=ts.Optimizer.fire,
    convergence_fn=force_convergence,
    init_kwargs={"cell_filter": ts.CellFilter.unit},
)
```

Sources: [high_level_tutorial.py](examples/tutorials/high_level_tutorial.py#L352-L412), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L485-L547), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L551-L570)

## Batched and Automatic Batching

The defining capability of TorchSim is batched execution. Pass a list of systems and the library simulates all of them in a single GPU kernel launch. When your list exceeds available GPU memory, enable autobatching with `autobatcher=True` and TorchSim automatically partitions the workload.

```python
from ase.build import bulk

# Create multiple distinct systems
fe_atoms = bulk("Fe", "fcc", a=5.26, cubic=True)
cu_atoms = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=5.43, cubic=True)
si_atoms = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.43, cubic=True)

systems = [fe_atoms, cu_atoms, si_atoms]

# Simulate all three in parallel
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=systems,
    model=lj_model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=50,
    temperature=1500,
    timestep=0.002,
    autobatcher=True,  # Auto-partition if memory is exceeded
)

# Results come back in original order
final_atoms_list = final_state.to_atoms()
print(f"Simulated {len(final_atoms_list)} systems in parallel")
```

The same batching pattern applies to `optimize` and `static`. Each function handles the internal complexity of state splitting, batch iteration, and result reordering transparently.

Sources: [high_level_tutorial.py](examples/tutorials/high_level_tutorial.py#L228-L335), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L346-L370)

## High-Level API Summary

TorchSim exposes three runner functions that cover the vast majority of atomistic simulation workflows. Each accepts diverse input formats, supports optional trajectory reporting, and handles automatic batching.

| Function | Purpose | Key Parameters | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `integrate()` | Molecular dynamics | `integrator`, `n_steps`, `temperature`, `timestep` | Final `SimState` |
| `optimize()` | Geometry optimization | `optimizer`, `convergence_fn`, `max_steps` | Final `SimState` |
| `static()` | Single-point calculations | None (no evolution) | `list[dict]` of properties |

All three runners accept `system` as an **ASE Atoms** object, a **PyMatGen Structure**, a raw `SimState`, or a **list of any of these**. The `trajectory_reporter` parameter accepts either a `TrajectoryReporter` instance or a dictionary with at least a `"filenames"` key. The `autobatcher` parameter accepts `True` (auto-configure), `False` (no batching), or a custom `BinningAutoBatcher`/`InFlightAutoBatcher` instance for fine-grained control.

> [!TIP]
> All models in TorchSim use the **MetalUnits** system internally (Å for distance, eV for energy, amu for mass, ps for time). The runner functions accept human-readable values — temperature in Kelvin, timestep in picoseconds — and convert them automatically. When using the low-level API directly, you must apply `MetalUnits.temperature` and `MetalUnits.time` conversions manually.

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L252-L270), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L551-L570), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L734-L760), [units.py](torch_sim/units.py#L84-L104)

## Supported Models

TorchSim ships with both classical pair potentials for quick prototyping and wrappers for state-of-the-art machine learning interatomic potentials. All models implement the `ModelInterface` abstract class, ensuring a uniform calling convention across the entire ecosystem.

| Category | Model | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Classical** | `LennardJonesModel` | Built-in, no dependencies |
| **Classical** | `MorseModel` | Built-in, no dependencies |
| **Classical** | `SoftSphereModel` | Built-in, no dependencies |
| **MLIP** | `MaceModel` (MACE, MACE-MPA) | Requires `mace-torch` |
| **MLIP** | `SevenNetModel` | Requires `sevenn` |
| **MLIP** | `ORBModel` | Requires `orb-models` |
| **MLIP** | `MatterSimModel` | Requires `matsciml` |
| **MLIP** | `FairChemModel` | Requires `fairchem-core` |
| **MLIP** | `NequipModel` | Requires `nequip` |
| **MLIP** | `MetatomicModel` (MatPES, CHGNet, etc.) | Requires `metatensor` |

> [!TIP]
> Start with `LennardJonesModel` for development and testing — it runs on CPU instantly with zero external dependencies. Switch to an MLIP model for production accuracy. The model interface is identical, so swapping models requires changing only the constructor call.

Sources: [models/interface.py](torch_sim/models/interface.py#L38-L137), [models/lennard_jones.py](torch_sim/models/lennard_jones.py#L74-L107), [models/__init__.py](torch_sim/models/__init__.py#L1-L2)

# Installation and Model Setup



This page walks you through installing TorchSim and configuring your first model — whether it is a production-grade machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) or a lightweight classical potential for prototyping. By the end, you will have a working simulation pipeline ready to run batched molecular dynamics or geometry optimizations.

## Prerequisites

TorchSim requires **Python 3.12 or later** and **PyTorch 2.0+**. Because TorchSim compiles no native extensions itself, the main prerequisite is simply having a compatible PyTorch installation that matches your CUDA version when running on GPU. You can verify your environment with:

```bash
python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"
```

The project targets three Python versions — 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14 — as declared in its classifier metadata.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L18-L28)

## Installation Methods

TorchSim offers two primary installation paths. Choose the one that matches your workflow.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Choose Installation] --> B{Production or Development?}
    B -->|Production| C[pip install from PyPI]
    B -->|Development| D[Clone & install from source]
    C --> E[Install MLIP extras]
    D --> F[pip install -e .]
    F --> G[Install prek for linting]
    E --> H[Ready to simulate]
    G --> H
```

### Installing from PyPI

The recommended approach for most users is a single pip command. The base package includes the simulation engine, classical potentials (Lennard-Jones, Morse, soft sphere, particle life), and the pair potential framework — everything you need to start simulating immediately without any MLIP dependency:

```bash
pip install torch-sim-atomistic
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L108-L112), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L29-L37)

### Installing from Source

If you want the latest unreleased features or plan to contribute, install in editable mode from a cloned repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/TorchSim/torch-sim
cd torch-sim
pip install -e .
```

The build backend is `uv_build`, so you need `uv` (version 0.7.12+) available if building from an sdist. For contributor workflows, installing the `prek` pre-commit hooks ensures that every commit passes ruff linting and ty type checking:

```bash
prek install
```

Sources: [docs/dev/dev_install.md](docs/dev/dev_install.md#L15-L21), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L79-L85)

### Verifying the Installation

After installation, confirm that TorchSim loads correctly and can access the GPU:

```py
import torch_sim as ts
print(f"TorchSim {ts.__version__} loaded successfully")
```

## Installing MLIP Model Extras

MLIP models are distributed as **optional extras** to keep the base installation lightweight. Each model has its own dependency group, so you install only what you need. All extras follow the same pattern:

```bash
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[<model_name>]
```

The following table lists every supported MLIP model, its pip extra, the upstream package it pulls in, and a minimal initialization snippet.

| Model | Extra | Upstream Package | Install Command |
|-------|-------|-----------------|-----------------|
| **MACE** | `mace` | `mace-torch>=0.3.15` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mace]` |
| **FairChem** | `fairchem` | `fairchem-core>=2.7` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[fairchem]` |
| **SevenNet** | `sevennet` | `sevenn[torchsim]>=0.12.1` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[sevennet]` |
| **MatterSim** | `mattersim` | `mattersim>=0.1.2` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mattersim]` |
| **Metatomic** | `metatomic` | `metatomic-torch>=0.1.3` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[metatomic]` |
| **ORB** | `orb` | `orb-models>=0.6.0` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[orb]` |
| **GraphPES** | `graphpes` | `graph-pes>=0.1`, `mace-torch>=0.3.12` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[graphpes]` |
| **NequIP** | `nequip` | `nequip>=0.17.0` | `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[nequip]` |

Beyond MLIPs, two additional extras provide interoperability and symmetry analysis:

| Extra | Purpose | Dependencies |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `io` | ASE, Pymatgen, Phonopy integration | `ase>=3.26`, `phonopy>=2.37.0`, `pymatgen>=2025.6.14` |
| `symmetry` | Crystal symmetry operations | `moyopy>=0.7.8` |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L39-L74)

> [!TIP]
> **Multiple extras at once:** You can combine extras in a single install: `pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mace,io,symmetry]`. However, see the next section carefully — some MLIP extras are mutually exclusive due to incompatible `e3nn` versions.

### Understanding Extra Conflicts

Several MLIP extras depend on different versions of the `e3nn` library, making them **mutually exclusive**. The project explicitly declares these conflicts in its configuration so that package managers like `uv` will warn or error if you attempt an impossible combination:

```mermaid
graph TD
    FC["FairChem"] -.->|conflict| GP["GraphPES"]
    FC -.->|conflict| MACE["MACE"]
    GP -.->|conflict| MS["MatterSim"]
    GP -.->|conflict| NQ["NequIP"]
    GP -.->|conflict| SN["SevenNet"]
    MACE -.->|conflict| MS
    MACE -.->|conflict| NQ
    MACE -.->|conflict| SN

    style FC fill:#f66
    style GP fill:#f66
    style MACE fill:#f66
    style MS fill:#69f
    style NQ fill:#69f
    style SN fill:#69f

    classDef conflict stroke:#f00,stroke-dasharray:5 5
    class FC,GP,MACE,MS,NQ,SN conflict
```

The conflict groups partition the MLIP landscape into two clusters that cannot coexist in the same environment:

| Cluster | Compatible Extras |
|---------|------------------|
| **Cluster A** (fairchem side) | `fairchem` alone (no other MLIPs) |
| **Cluster B** (mace/graphpes side) | Any subset of `{mace, graphpes, mattersim, sevennet, nequip}` — but `graphpes` also conflicts with `mattersim`, `nequip`, and `sevennet` |
| **Independent** | `metatomic`, `orb` — no conflicts with any other extra |

The practical takeaway: **pick one MLIP per virtual environment**, or use `metatomic`/`orb` which have no conflicts. If you need to switch between conflicting models, use separate conda environments or virtualenvs.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L142-L186)

## Setting Up Your First Model

All models in TorchSim implement the `ModelInterface` abstract base class, which inherits from `torch.nn.Module`. Every model's `forward()` method accepts a `SimState` and returns a dictionary containing at minimum `"energy"` (shape `[n_systems]`) and `"forces"` (shape `[n_atoms, 3]`), with optional `"stress"` (shape `[n_systems, 3, 3]`). This uniform interface means you can swap any model into the same simulation pipeline without code changes.

![TorchSim package treemap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TorchSim/torch-sim/main/docs/_static/torch-sim-pkg-treemap.svg)

### Classical Potentials (No Extra Install Required)

Classical potentials ship with the base package and require zero additional dependencies. They are ideal for testing, prototyping, and educational use.

**Lennard-Jones** models pairwise van der Waals interactions with the standard 12-6 form:

```py
import torch
import torch_sim as ts

# No extra install needed — ships with base package
model = ts.models.LennardJonesModel(
    sigma=3.405,    # Å (argon-like)
    epsilon=0.0104,  # eV
    device=torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"),
)
```

**Morse** potentials add an exponential decay term useful for modeling bond stretching:

```py
model = ts.models.MorseModel(
    sigma=2.55,     # equilibrium distance (Å)
    epsilon=0.436,  # well depth (eV)
    alpha=1.359,    # width parameter
)
```

**Soft Sphere** potentials provide a purely repulsive interaction, useful for granular and hard-sphere simulations:

```py
model = ts.models.SoftSphereModel(
    sigma=1.0,
    epsilon=1.0,
    alpha=2.0,      # steepness of repulsion
)
```

For **multi-component systems** with species-dependent parameters, use `SoftSphereMultiModel` which accepts full interaction matrices:

```py
model = ts.models.SoftSphereMultiModel(
    atomic_numbers=torch.tensor([18, 36]),  # Ar, Kr
    sigma_matrix=torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.8], [0.8, 0.6]]),
    epsilon_matrix=torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.5], [0.5, 2.0]]),
)
```

For fully **custom pair potentials**, the `PairPotentialModel` framework accepts any Python function matching the signature `pair_fn(distances, atomic_numbers_i, atomic_numbers_j) -> pair_energies` and automatically computes forces via autograd:

```py
import functools

def bmhtf_pair(dr, zi, zj, A, B, C, D, sigma):
    """Born-Meyer-Huggins-Tosi-Fumi ionic potential."""
    exp_term = A * torch.exp(B * (sigma - dr))
    r6_term = C / dr.pow(6)
    r8_term = D / dr.pow(8)
    return torch.where(dr > 0, exp_term - r6_term - r8_term, torch.zeros_like(dr))

fn = functools.partial(bmhtf_pair, A=20.35, B=3.15, C=674.48, D=837.08, sigma=2.755)
model = ts.models.PairPotentialModel(pair_fn=fn, cutoff=10.0)
```

Sources: [torch_sim/models/lennard_jones.py](torch_sim/models/lennard_jones.py#L74-L107), [torch_sim/models/morse.py](torch_sim/models/morse.py#L78-L112), [torch_sim/models/soft_sphere.py](torch_sim/models/soft_sphere.py#L175-L209), [torch_sim/models/pair_potential.py](torch_sim/models/pair_potential.py#L283-L321)

### MLIP Models

Each MLIP wrapper follows a similar pattern: install the extra, load the upstream model, and wrap it in the TorchSim adapter. Below are setup examples for the most commonly used models.

**MACE** — high-accuracy equivariant architecture supporting both checkpoint files and in-memory `torch.nn.Module` objects. It supports optional CuEq acceleration for faster inference:

```py
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mace]
```

```py
from mace.calculators.foundations_models import mace_mp
from torch_sim.models.mace import MaceModel

# Load a pretrained MACE foundation model
mace = mace_mp(model="small", return_raw_model=True)
model = MaceModel(
    model=mace,
    device=torch.device("cuda"),
    dtype=torch.float64,
    compute_stress=True,    # needed for NPT simulations
    enable_cueq=False,      # set True for CuEq acceleration
)
```

**FairChem** — supports pretrained model names and local checkpoint paths, using an optimized batch predictor API:

```py
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[fairchem]
```

```py
from torch_sim.models.fairchem import FairChemModel

model = FairChemModel(
    model="EquiformerV2-31M-S2EF-OC20-All-MD",  # pretrained name
    device=torch.device("cuda"),
    compute_stress=True,
)
```

**SevenNet** and **ORB** follow a re-export pattern — the actual `ModelInterface` implementation lives in the upstream package, and TorchSim re-exports it with backward-compatible naming:

```py
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[sevennet]
```

```py
from torch_sim.models import SevenNetModel

model = SevenNetModel(device=torch.device("cuda"))
```

```py
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[orb]
```

```py
from torch_sim.models import OrbModel

model = OrbModel(device=torch.device("cuda"))
```

**Metatomic** — supports the pre-defined `pet-mad` model by name, or custom `.ckpt`/`.pt` checkpoint files. It validates that the model supports the requested device:

```py
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[metatomic]
```

```py
from torch_sim.models.metatomic import MetatomicModel

model = MetatomicModel(
    model="pet-mad",   # downloads from HuggingFace automatically
    device=torch.device("cuda"),
    compute_stress=True,
)
```

**MatterSim** — requires an already-loaded MatterSim `Potential` object to be passed in:

```py
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mattersim]
```

```py
from mattersim.forcefield import MatterSimCalculator
from torch_sim.models.mattersim import MatterSimModel

# Load via MatterSim's own API first
calculator = MatterSimCalculator()
model = MatterSimModel(
    model=calculator.potential,
    device=torch.device("cuda"),
)
```

Sources: [torch_sim/models/mace.py](torch_sim/models/mace.py#L103-L168), [torch_sim/models/fairchem.py](torch_sim/models/fairchem.py#L71-L152), [torch_sim/models/sevennet.py](torch_sim/models/sevennet.py#L15-L17), [torch_sim/models/orb.py](torch_sim/models/orb.py#L15-L27), [torch_sim/models/metatomic.py](torch_sim/models/metatomic.py#L62-L141), [torch_sim/models/mattersim.py](torch_sim/models/mattersim.py#L55-L114)

### Model Interface Contract

Regardless of which model you choose, every TorchSim model implements `ModelInterface` and exposes four key properties:

| Property | Type | Purpose |
|----------|------|---------|
| `device` | `torch.device` | Where computation runs (CPU or CUDA) |
| `dtype` | `torch.dtype` | Tensor precision (typically `float32` or `float64`) |
| `compute_stress` | `bool` | Whether stress tensor is returned in `forward()` output |
| `compute_forces` | `bool` | Whether atomic forces are computed |

The `forward()` method returns a dictionary with this structure:

```py
output = model(sim_state)
# output = {
#     "energy": tensor of shape [n_systems],
#     "forces": tensor of shape [n_atoms, 3],
#     "stress": tensor of shape [n_systems, 3, 3],  # only if compute_stress=True
# }
```

> [!TIP]
> **Stress computation matters.** If you plan to run NPT simulations (constant pressure) or cell optimizations, make sure `compute_stress=True` is set during model initialization. For NVE/NVT dynamics with fixed cells, you can disable it for a small performance gain.

Sources: [torch_sim/models/interface.py](torch_sim/models/interface.py#L38-L169)

## Quick Validation Pipeline

After installing and setting up a model, verify the entire pipeline end-to-end with this minimal script:

```py
import torch
import torch_sim as ts
from ase.build import bulk

# 1. Choose your model (swap this single line for any model above)
model = ts.models.LennardJonesModel(sigma=3.405, epsilon=0.0104)

# 2. Build initial atomic structure
atoms = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.58, cubic=True).repeat((2, 2, 2))

# 3. Convert to SimState
state = ts.initialize_state(atoms, model=model)

# 4. Run a short NVT simulation
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=state,
    model=model,
    n_steps=20,
    timestep=0.002,
    temperature=300,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
)

print(f"Final energy: {final_state.energy}")
```

## Optional Extras for a Complete Workflow

For production simulations, you will likely want file I/O and symmetry analysis in addition to your MLIP:

```bash
pip install torch-sim-atomistic[mace,io,symmetry]
```

The `io` extra unlocks ASE `Atoms` ↔ `SimState` conversion, Pymatgen structure support, and Phonopy integration. The `symmetry` extra provides crystallographic symmetry operations for symmetric cell handling. Together with an MLIP extra, this gives you a full-featured simulation environment.

Now that TorchSim is installed and you have a model ready, the natural next steps are:

- **[Running Batched MD Simulations](4-running-batched-md-simulations)** — learn how to run multiple independent simulations simultaneously on GPU, leveraging TorchSim's automatic batching for massive throughput gains.
- **[Running Batched Geometry Optimizations](5-running-batched-geometry-optimizations)** — relax atomic positions and unit cells using FIRE, L-BFGS, or gradient descent optimizers across dozens of structures at once.

# Running Batched MD Simulations



TorchSim enables you to simulate dozens to thousands of molecular systems simultaneously on a single GPU, turning what would be hours of serial computation into minutes of parallel execution. This page walks through both the high-level `integrate()` runner API and the lower-level init/step pattern, covering ensemble selection, temperature scheduling, trajectory reporting, and automatic memory management for batched workloads that exceed GPU capacity.

## Architecture Overview

The batched MD pipeline in TorchSim follows a layered architecture where the high-level runner orchestrates state initialization, integrator selection, batch iteration, and trajectory reporting. At its core, every MD simulation passes through the same two-phase lifecycle: **initialization** (converting raw atomic structures into an `MDState` with momenta, forces, and energy) followed by **time-stepping** (repeatedly advancing the state by one timestep). When autobatching is enabled, this lifecycle is applied to memory-sized sub-batches, and the results are reassembled into a single unified state at the end.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input["Input Layer"]
        A["ASE Atoms / pymatgen Structures<br/>lists of mixed systems"]
    end

    subgraph Runner["ts.integrate() Runner"]
        B["initialize_state()<br/>→ SimState"]
        C["_normalize_temperature_tensor()<br/>→ kT tensor (n_steps, n_systems)"]
        D{"autobatcher?"}
        D -->|False| E["Single batch loop"]
        D -->|True| F["BinningAutoBatcher<br/>memory-aware binning"]
        F --> G["Batch 1 → init → step loop"]
        F --> H["Batch 2 → init → step loop"]
        F --> I["Batch N → init → step loop"]
        G --> J["restore_original_order()"]
        H --> J
        I --> J
        E --> K["init → step loop"]
    end

    subgraph Output["Output Layer"]
        J --> L["concatenate_states()<br/>→ Final MDState"]
        K --> L
        M["TrajectoryReporter<br/>→ HDF5 files"]
    end

    A --> B
    B --> C
    C --> D
    G --> M
    H --> M
    K --> M
    L --> N["final_state.to_atoms()<br/>final_state.to_structures()"]
```

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L252-L405), [integrators/__init__.py](torch_sim/integrators/__init__.py#L1-L175)

## The `integrate()` Function

The `integrate()` function is the primary entry point for running batched molecular dynamics. It accepts atomic systems in any format that TorchSim understands (ASE `Atoms`, pymatgen `Structure`, or already-initialized `SimState`), a model implementing the `ModelInterface`, and configuration for the integrator ensemble, temperature schedule, and timestep.

```python
import torch_sim as ts

final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=ase_atoms_or_list,
    model=my_model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=10_000,
    temperature=1000.0,          # Kelvin
    timestep=0.002,               # picoseconds
)
```

The `system` argument accepts a single atomic structure or a list of structures. When a list is provided, TorchSim concatenates them into a single batched `SimState` with a `system_idx` tensor mapping each atom to its parent system. All systems in a batch are advanced through the same number of timesteps using the same model, but each can have its own temperature schedule (see the temperature section below). The function returns a single `MDState` containing the final positions, momenta, forces, and energy for every system in the batch.

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L252-L405), [state.py](torch_sim/state.py#L1054-L1197)

## Available Integrators

TorchSim provides eight integrators spanning three thermodynamic ensembles, all registered in the `Integrator` enum and `INTEGRATOR_REGISTRY`. Each integrator is implemented as a pair of functions: an `_init` function that creates the appropriate `MDState` subclass (initializing momenta, forces, and any ensemble-specific state variables), and a `_step` function that advances the state by one timestep.

| Integrator Key | Ensemble | Thermostat / Barostat | State Class | Key Keyword Args |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `nve` | Microcanonical | None (energy conserved) | `MDState` | — |
| `nvt_langevin` | Canonical | Langevin (BAOAB splitting) | `MDState` | `gamma` (friction) |
| `nvt_vrescale` | Canonical | Velocity rescaling (Bussi) | `NVTVRescaleState` | `tau` (coupling time) |
| `nvt_nose_hoover` | Canonical | Nosé-Hoover chain | `NVTNoseHooverState` | `tau`, `chain_length`, `chain_steps` |
| `npt_langevin` | Isobaric-isothermal | Langevin barostat | `NPTLangevinState` | `gamma`, `external_pressure`, `alpha` |
| `npt_nose_hoover` | Isobaric-isothermal | Nosé-Hoover barostat | `NPTNoseHooverState` | `external_pressure`, `t_tau`, `b_tau` |
| `npt_isotropic_crescale` | Isobaric-isothermal | C-Rescale (isotropic) | `NPTCRescaleState` | `external_pressure`, `tau_p` |
| `npt_anisotropic_crescale` | Isobaric-isothermal | C-Rescale (anisotropic) | `NPTCRescaleState` | `external_pressure`, `tau_p` |

NPT integrators require the model to have `compute_stress=True`, since they need the stress tensor to compute pressure forces on the cell. All NVT and NPT integrators accept the `init_kwargs` parameter in `integrate()` for passing ensemble-specific initialization arguments such as `tau` or `chain_length`, while ensemble-specific stepping arguments like `external_pressure` or `gamma` are passed via `**integrator_kwargs`.

> [!TIP]
> When choosing an integrator, prefer `nvt_langevin` or `npt_langevin` for production runs: Langevin dynamics are stochastic and robustly sample the canonical distribution without fine-tuning thermostat parameters. Use Nosé-Hoover variants when you need deterministic, time-reversible trajectories (e.g., for computing transport properties). The `nve` integrator is useful for energy conservation tests and microcanonical benchmarking.

Sources: [integrators/__init__.py](torch_sim/integrators/__init__.py#L97-L175), [nvt.py](torch_sim/integrators/nvt.py#L24-L629), [npt.py](torch_sim/integrators/npt.py#L26-L635)

## Temperature Scheduling

The `temperature` parameter in `integrate()` is remarkably flexible. Rather than accepting only a scalar, it supports four scheduling patterns that control how temperature varies over time and across systems:

| Pattern | Input Shape | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Constant | `float` or `tensor(1)` | Same temperature for all steps and all systems |
| Per-system | `tensor(n_systems)` | Each system has its own temperature, held constant over all steps |
| Per-step | `tensor(n_steps)` | Temperature changes at each step, applied uniformly to all systems |
| Per-step per-system | `tensor(n_steps, n_systems)` | Full schedule: each system has its own temperature at each step |

Internally, `_normalize_temperature_tensor()` converts any of these inputs into a tensor of shape `(n_steps,)` or `(n_steps, n_systems)` and scales it by the metal unit system's temperature factor (eV/K). When a per-system temperature array has the same length as `n_steps`, TorchSim emits a warning since the intent is ambiguous, defaulting to per-system interpretation.

This scheduling system enables powerful workflows: simulated annealing (linearly decreasing temperature array), replica exchange (different temperatures per system within the same batch), and temperature-jump experiments — all without modifying the integrator itself.

```python
# Linear cooling from 2000K to 300K over 5000 steps
temps = torch.linspace(2000, 300, 5000)
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=atoms, model=model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=5000, temperature=temps, timestep=0.002,
)
```

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L173-L227)

## Trajectory Reporting

TorchSim provides a built-in `TrajectoryReporter` that writes simulation data to HDF5 files during integration. The simplest way to enable it is to pass a dictionary with filenames:

```python
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=atoms, model=model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=5000, temperature=1000, timestep=0.002,
    trajectory_reporter={"filenames": "trajectory.h5"},
)
```

When autobatching is enabled, each system in the batch gets its own trajectory file, and the reporter automatically reopens the correct files for each sub-batch. For finer control, instantiate the `TrajectoryReporter` directly to configure the state saving frequency, property calculators (custom per-step quantities like kinetic energy, temperature, or pressure), and trajectory compression settings.

After the simulation, read trajectory data with `TorchSimTrajectory`:

```python
with ts.TorchSimTrajectory("trajectory.h5") as traj:
    energies = traj.get_array("potential_energy")
    final_atoms = traj.get_atoms(-1)
```

Sources: [trajectory.py](torch_sim/trajectory.py#L69-L464), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L34-L68)

## Automatic Batching for Large Workloads

When simulating many systems whose combined atom count exceeds GPU memory, set `autobatcher=True` to let TorchSim automatically partition the batch into memory-safe sub-batches. The `integrate()` function uses the `BinningAutoBatcher` strategy, which groups systems using a bin-packing algorithm that minimizes the total number of batches while keeping each batch within the GPU's memory budget.

```python
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=many_atoms,  # e.g., 100 systems
    model=mace_model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=5000, temperature=1000, timestep=0.002,
    autobatcher=True,  # automatically manage GPU memory
)
```

The autobatcher first calls `estimate_max_memory_scaler()` to determine the largest memory metric the model can handle on the current GPU, then packs systems into bins such that the sum of memory metrics in each bin stays below this threshold. Memory scaling is estimated based on the `memory_scales_with` property of the model — most MLIPs with radial cutoffs use `"n_atoms_x_density"`, while models with fixed neighbor counts use `"n_atoms"`. Each sub-batch runs the full init → step loop independently, and the final states are reassembled via `restore_original_order()` and `concatenate_states()` to produce a single output state.

> [!TIP]
> The `max_memory_scaler` is typically fixed for a given model and GPU. After the first run determines it via auto-detection, you can cache this value and pass a pre-configured `BinningAutoBatcher(model, max_memory_scaler=cached_value)` to avoid the slow calibration step on subsequent runs. This is particularly valuable in production pipelines that run repeatedly with the same hardware and model.

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L71-L107), [autobatching.py](torch_sim/autobatching.py#L520-L768), [interface.py](torch_sim/models/interface.py#L125-L133)

## Low-Level Init/Step Pattern

For advanced workflows that need direct control over the integration loop — such as custom logging, conditional logic between steps, or coupling with external processes — you can bypass `integrate()` and use the init/step functions directly. Each integrator follows the same two-function contract: `_init` transforms a `SimState` into the appropriate `MDState` subclass, and `_step` advances it by one timestep.

```python
# Low-level NVT Langevin with custom per-step logic
import torch
from torch_sim.units import MetalUnits as U

kT = torch.tensor(1000 * U.temperature)
dt = torch.tensor(0.002 * U.time)

state = ts.initialize_state(ase_atoms, model.device, model.dtype)
state = ts.nvt_langevin_init(state, model, kT=kT)

for step in range(10_000):
    state = ts.nvt_langevin_step(state, model, dt=dt, kT=kT, gamma=1.0 / U.time)

    if step % 500 == 0:
        temp = state.calc_temperature()
        print(f"Step {step}: T = {temp.item():.1f} K")
```

The low-level pattern also supports batched states directly. When you pass a batched `SimState` to `nvt_langevin_init`, all systems are initialized with momenta drawn from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at the specified temperature, and `nvt_langevin_step` advances every system simultaneously within a single GPU kernel launch.

Sources: [nvt.py](torch_sim/integrators/nvt.py#L86-L195), [nve.py](torch_sim/integrators/nve.py#L17-L105), [md.py](torch_sim/integrators/md.py#L20-L100)

## Mixed-System Batching

One of TorchSim's most powerful features is the ability to batch **different** systems — different elements, different structures, different sizes — into a single simulation. The `system_idx` tensor in `SimState` tracks which atoms belong to which system, and all integrators use this index for per-system temperature control, degree-of-freedom calculations, and property reporting.

```python
from ase.build import bulk, molecule

si_bulk = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.43).repeat((2, 2, 2))
cu_bulk = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.61).repeat((3, 3, 3))
h2o = molecule("H2O")

# All three systems simulated simultaneously at different temperatures
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=[si_bulk, cu_bulk, h2o],
    model=mace_model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=5000,
    temperature=[1500.0, 300.0, 300.0],  # per-system temperatures
    timestep=0.002,
)
```

Each system in the batch maintains independent state: separate cells, separate momenta, separate energies. The MLIP model receives the concatenated batch and returns forces for all atoms in a single forward pass, which is where the GPU efficiency comes from — the model's fixed overhead (kernel launches, memory allocations) is amortized across all systems in the batch.

Sources: [state.py](torch_sim/state.py#L70-L135), [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L335-L350)

## Putting It All Together

The following example combines all the concepts covered on this page — batched multi-system simulation with autobatching, trajectory reporting, and temperature scheduling:

```python
import torch
import torch_sim as ts
from ase.build import bulk

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# Set up a MACE model
from mace.calculators.foundations_models import mace_mp
from torch_sim.models.mace import MaceModel

mace = mace_mp(model="small", return_raw_model=True)
model = MaceModel(model=mace, device=device)

# Create diverse systems to batch together
systems = [
    bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.43).repeat((2, 2, 2)),
    bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.61).repeat((3, 3, 3)),
    bulk("Al", "fcc", a=4.05).repeat((2, 2, 2)),
] * 10  # 30 systems total

# Run with automatic batching and trajectory reporting
final_state = ts.integrate(
    system=systems,
    model=model,
    integrator=ts.Integrator.nvt_langevin,
    n_steps=5000,
    temperature=[800.0, 300.0, 300.0],  # per-system (broadcast over steps)
    timestep=0.002,
    trajectory_reporter={"filenames": [f"traj_{i}.h5" for i in range(30)]},
    autobatcher=True,
)
```

# Running Batched Geometry Optimizations



This page covers how to perform geometry optimizations — relaxing atomic positions and optionally unit cells — across batches of molecular systems simultaneously on GPU. TorchSim's optimization framework follows a filter-based architecture where optimization algorithms operate independently from cell parameterization, and both layers support fully batched execution. Whether you need to relax a handful of defect structures or thousands of DFT-generated candidates, the same API scales from single systems to large batches with automatic GPU memory management.

## Optimization Architecture Overview

TorchSim's geometry optimization system is built around three pillars: a **state hierarchy** that tracks per-system optimization state, an **init/step protocol** that separates initialization from iteration, and a **cell filter abstraction** that decouples cell optimization from position optimization. These layers compose so that any optimizer can run with or without cell relaxation, on any batch size, with or without automatic memory batching.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "High-Level API"
        OPT["ts.optimize()"]
        OPT -->|"delegates"| IFB["InFlightAutoBatcher"]
        OPT -->|"uses"| CONV["convergence_fn"]
    end

    subgraph "Optimizer Layer"
        FIRE["FIRE<br/>(fire_init / fire_step)"]
        GD["Gradient Descent<br/>(gradient_descent_init / gradient_descent_step)"]
        LBFGS["L-BFGS<br/>(lbfgs_init / lbfgs_step)"]
        BFGS["BFGS<br/>(bfgs_init / bfgs_step)"]
    end

    subgraph "Cell Filter Layer"
        UCF["Unit Cell Filter"]
        FCF["Frechet Cell Filter"]
    end

    subgraph "State Hierarchy"
        OPT_S["OptimState"]
        FIRE_S["FireState"]
        LBFGS_S["LBFGSState"]
        BFGS_S["BFGSState"]
        CELL_S["CellOptimState"]
        CELL_FIRE["CellFireState"]
        CELL_LBFGS["CellLBFGSState"]
        CELL_BFGS["CellBFGSState"]
    end

    OPT --> FIRE & GD & LBFGS & BFGS
    FIRE & LBFGS & BFGS --> UCF & FCF
    OPT_S --> FIRE_S & LBFGS_S & BFGS_S
    CELL_S --> CELL_FIRE & CELL_LBFGS & CELL_BFGS
    FIRE_S -.->|"+ CellOptimState"| CELL_FIRE
    LBFGS_S -.->|"+ CellOptimState"| CELL_LBFGS
    BFGS_S -.->|"+ CellOptimState"| CELL_BFGS
```

The `Optimizer` enum and `OPTIM_REGISTRY` dictionary in [optimizers/__init__.py](torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py#L38-L53) provide a string-keyed lookup mapping each optimizer name to its `(init_fn, step_fn)` tuple. The high-level `optimize()` runner accepts either an `Optimizer` enum value or a raw `(init_fn, step_fn)` tuple, giving you flexibility to use built-in or custom optimizers interchangeably.

Sources: [optimizers/__init__.py](torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py#L38-L53), [optimizers/state.py](torch_sim/optimizers/state.py#L11-L25)

## Available Optimizers

TorchSim ships four optimization algorithms, each with different convergence characteristics and computational costs. All four operate on batched states identically — you never need to loop over systems manually.

| Optimizer | Enum Key | State Class | Best For | Complexity |
|-----------|----------|-------------|----------|------------|
| Gradient Descent | `Optimizer.gradient_descent` | `OptimState` | Debugging, simple test cases | O(N) per step |
| FIRE | `Optimizer.fire` | `FireState` | General-purpose relaxation | O(N) per step |
| L-BFGS | `Optimizer.lbfgs` | `LBFGSState` | Large systems, quasi-Newton convergence | O(N × history) per step |
| BFGS | `Optimizer.bfgs` | `BFGSState` | Small-to-moderate systems, best convergence | O(N²) memory |

**FIRE** (Fast Inertial Relaxation Engine) is the default workhorse. It combines molecular dynamics-like velocity updates with adaptive damping, making it robust for a wide range of initial conditions. It comes in two flavors: `"ase_fire"` (ASE-compatible, default) and `"vv_fire"` (velocity-Verlet based). FIRE is implemented in [fire.py](torch_sim/optimizers/fire.py#L22-L127).

**L-BFGS** approximates the inverse Hessian using a limited history of displacement-gradient pairs (default 20 steps), achieving superlinear convergence near minima while keeping memory linear in system size. It uses a fixed step size with the classical two-loop recursion for inverse-Hessian-vector products. See [lbfgs.py](torch_sim/optimizers/lbfgs.py#L114-L287).

**BFGS** maintains the full Hessian matrix (padded to `3*max_atoms × 3*max_atoms` per batch), giving the best convergence rate at O(N²) memory cost. This makes it ideal for systems with fewer than ~200 atoms. See [bfgs.py](torch_sim/optimizers/bfgs.py#L87-L256).

**Gradient Descent** applies a fixed learning rate to force directions. It is the simplest optimizer, useful for testing and as a baseline. See [gradient_descent.py](torch_sim/optimizers/gradient_descent.py#L18-L77).

> [!TIP]
> When optimizing systems with widely different atom counts in the same batch, L-BFGS and BFGS pad internal history/Hessian tensors to `max_atoms`. This is handled transparently by the state system — you don't need to sort or partition your systems by size. However, very heterogeneous batches (e.g., 10 atoms + 1000 atoms) waste GPU memory on padding. Consider grouping similarly-sized systems together for efficiency.

Sources: [optimizers/__init__.py](torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py#L38-L53), [fire.py](torch_sim/optimizers/fire.py#L22-L127), [lbfgs.py](torch_sim/optimizers/lbfgs.py#L114-L287), [bfgs.py](torch_sim/optimizers/bfgs.py#L87-L256)

## Quick Start: The High-Level `optimize()` Runner

The simplest way to run batched geometry optimization is through the `ts.optimize()` function. It handles optimizer initialization, convergence checking, automatic batching via the `InFlightAutoBatcher`, trajectory reporting, and progress tracking — all in a single call.

```python
import torch_sim as ts

# Prepare systems (list of ASE Atoms objects)
atoms_list = [si_structure, cu_structure, fe_structure]

# Use a model
result = ts.optimize(
    atoms_list,
    model=mace_model,
    optimizer=ts.Optimizer.fire,
    convergence_fn=ts.generate_force_convergence_fn(force_tol=0.05),
    max_steps=10_000,
    steps_between_swaps=5,
)
```

The `optimize()` function accepts `StateLike` inputs — ASE `Atoms`, Pymatgen `Structure`, or a `SimState` directly. When you pass non-`OptimState` objects, it automatically initializes the optimizer state via a chunked application that respects GPU memory limits. The function then enters a loop where it repeatedly: (1) requests the next batch from the `InFlightAutoBatcher`, (2) runs `steps_between_swaps` optimizer steps, (3) evaluates convergence, and (4) feeds the convergence tensor back to the batcher so converged states are swapped out and new ones are loaded in.

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L551-L730)

### Convergence Functions

The `optimize()` runner requires a convergence function that returns a boolean tensor of shape `(n_systems,)` — `True` where converged, `False` otherwise. TorchSim provides two built-in generators:

| Function | Criterion | Signature |
|----------|-----------|-----------|
| `generate_force_convergence_fn(force_tol)` | Max per-atom force < tolerance | Optional `include_cell_forces=True` for cell optimizations |
| `generate_energy_convergence_fn(energy_tol)` | \|ΔE\| < tolerance between steps | Compares current energy to previous step |

If you pass no `convergence_fn`, the optimizer defaults to energy convergence with `energy_tol=1e-3`. For production relaxations, force-based convergence is generally preferred because it directly measures the quality of the optimized geometry rather than indirect energy differences.

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L485-L547)

### Key Parameters of `optimize()`

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `optimizer` | `Optimizer` or `tuple` | required | Built-in optimizer enum or custom `(init_fn, step_fn)` |
| `convergence_fn` | `Callable` | energy at 1e-3 | Returns `(n_systems,)` boolean tensor |
| `max_steps` | `int` | 10,000 | Hard cap on total optimization steps |
| `steps_between_swaps` | `int` | 5 | Steps before checking convergence and swapping |
| `autobatcher` | `InFlightAutoBatcher` or `bool` | `False` | `True` enables auto memory estimation; pass instance for custom config |
| `trajectory_reporter` | `TrajectoryReporter` or `dict` | `None` | Enable trajectory logging |
| `init_kwargs` | `dict` | `None` | Extra kwargs forwarded to optimizer `init` function |
| `**optimizer_kwargs` | — | — | Extra kwargs forwarded to optimizer `step` function |

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L551-L564)

## Low-Level API: Init and Step Pattern

For finer control over the optimization loop — custom convergence logic, mixed optimizer strategies, or integration into larger workflows — use the init/step pattern directly. Every optimizer exposes an `_init` function that creates the appropriate state, and a `_step` function that advances it by one iteration.

```python
# 1. Convert your structures to a batched SimState
state = ts.io.atoms_to_state(atoms_list, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)

# 2. Initialize the optimizer (computes initial forces/energy)
state = ts.fire_init(state=state, model=mace_model, dt_start=0.005)

# 3. Run optimization steps manually
for step in range(500):
    state = ts.fire_step(state=state, model=mace_model, dt_max=0.01)
    max_force = ts.system_wise_max_force(state)
    if (max_force < 0.05).all():
        print(f"Converged at step {step}")
        break
```

Each `_init` function calls the model to compute initial forces and energy, then packages everything into the appropriate state dataclass. The `_step` function takes the current state and model, performs one optimization iteration, and returns the updated state. All tensors in the state are batched — `forces` has shape `(total_atoms, 3)`, `energy` has shape `(n_systems,)`, and so on.

Sources: [optimizers/__init__.py](torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py#L1-L10), [examples/scripts/2_structural_optimization.py](examples/scripts/2_structural_optimization.py#L113-L120)

### Optimizer-Specific Initialization Parameters

Each optimizer's `_init` function accepts configuration parameters that control its behavior:

**FIRE** ([fire_init](torch_sim/optimizers/fire.py#L22-L113)):
| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `dt_start` | 0.1 | Initial timestep |
| `alpha_start` | 0.1 | Initial mixing parameter |
| `fire_flavor` | `"ase_fire"` | `"ase_fire"` (ASE-compatible) or `"vv_fire"` (velocity-Verlet) |
| `cell_filter` | `None` | Cell filter for simultaneous cell optimization |

**L-BFGS** ([lbfgs_init](torch_sim/optimizers/lbfgs.py#L114-L278)):
| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `step_size` | 0.1 | Fixed step size for displacement |
| `alpha` | auto | Initial inverse Hessian scale (stiffness) |
| `cell_filter` | `None` | Cell filter for simultaneous cell optimization |

**BFGS** ([bfgs_init](torch_sim/optimizers/bfgs.py#L87-L251)):
| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `max_step` | 0.2 | Maximum displacement per atom per step |
| `alpha` | 70.0 | Initial Hessian scale (stiffness) |
| `cell_filter` | `None` | Cell filter for simultaneous cell optimization |

Sources: [fire.py](torch_sim/optimizers/fire.py#L22-L113), [lbfgs.py](torch_sim/optimizers/lbfgs.py#L114-L278), [bfgs.py](torch_sim/optimizers/bfgs.py#L87-L251)

## Cell Optimization with Filters

Many materials science workflows require simultaneous relaxation of atomic positions **and** unit cell parameters. TorchSim handles this through **cell filters** — composable wrappers that extend any optimizer to include cell degrees of freedom. The filter handles computing cell forces from the stress tensor, applying strain constraints, and updating the cell matrix, while the underlying optimizer treats everything as a unified optimization problem.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Without Cell Filter"
        A1["SimState"] --> B1["OptimState"]
        B1 --> C1["Positions only"]
    end

    subgraph "With Cell Filter"
        A2["SimState"] --> B2["CellOptimState"]
        B2 --> C2["Positions + Cell DOFs"]
    end
```

The `CellFilter` enum in [cell_filters.py](torch_sim/optimizers/cell_filters.py#L287-L293) provides two options:

| Filter | Description | Best For |
|--------|-------------|----------|
| `CellFilter.unit` | Transforms cell via logarithmic deformation gradient; directly controls strain. | General cell relaxation, isotropic or anisotropic |
| `CellFilter.frechet` | Uses the Frechet derivative of cell energy for cell forces; compatible with ASE's `FrechetCellFilter`. | Matching ASE behavior, non-orthogonal cells |

Cell filters are passed to any optimizer's `_init` function:

```python
# FIRE with Frechet cell filter
state = ts.fire_init(
    state=state, model=model,
    cell_filter=ts.CellFilter.frechet,
    scalar_pressure=0.0,  # GPa
)

for step in range(500):
    state = ts.fire_step(state=state, model=model)
```

When a cell filter is active, the optimizer's internal state is automatically upgraded to the corresponding `Cell*State` variant (`CellFireState`, `CellBFGSState`, `CellLBFGSState`). These composite states inherit both the cell filter attributes (`reference_cell`, `cell_forces`, `cell_factor`, `hydrostatic_strain`, `constant_volume`) and the optimizer-specific attributes (velocities for FIRE, Hessian for BFGS, history for L-BFGS).

For gradient descent with cell optimization, separate learning rates control positions and cell:

```python
state = ts.gradient_descent_init(
    state=state, model=model,
    cell_filter=ts.CellFilter.unit,
)
for step in range(500):
    state = ts.gradient_descent_step(
        state=state, model=model,
        pos_lr=0.01, cell_lr=0.1,
    )
```

> [!TIP]
> When using cell filters with quasi-Newton methods (BFGS/L-BFGS), forces and positions are internally transformed into the filter's scaled coordinate space. The `prev_forces` and `prev_positions` stored in the state are in this transformed space, matching ASE's `UnitCellFilter`/`FrechetCellFilter` behavior for result reproducibility. Set `include_cell_forces=True` in `generate_force_convergence_fn()` to ensure both atomic and cell forces converge.

Sources: [cell_filters.py](torch_sim/optimizers/cell_filters.py#L287-L527), [gradient_descent.py](torch_sim/optimizers/gradient_descent.py#L70-L77)

## Complete Example: Batched FIRE with Cell Relaxation

This example demonstrates a realistic batched optimization workflow — relaxing three different crystal structures (Si, Cu, Fe) simultaneously with both position and cell degrees of freedom, using the high-level `optimize()` runner with automatic memory management.

```python
import torch
import torch_sim as ts
from ase.build import bulk
import numpy as np

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# --- 1. Create perturbed structures ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=0)
si = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.21, cubic=True).repeat((2, 2, 2))
si.positions += 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(si.positions.shape)

cu = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.85).repeat((2, 2, 2))
cu.positions += 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(cu.positions.shape)

fe = bulk("Fe", "bcc", a=2.95).repeat((2, 2, 2))
fe.positions += 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(fe.positions.shape)

atoms_list = [si, cu, fe]

# --- 2. Run batched optimization ---
result = ts.optimize(
    atoms_list,
    model=mace_model,
    optimizer=ts.Optimizer.fire,
    convergence_fn=ts.generate_force_convergence_fn(force_tol=0.05),
    max_steps=10_000,
    steps_between_swaps=5,
    autobatcher=True,           # auto GPU memory management
    init_kwargs={"cell_filter": ts.CellFilter.frechet},
    trajectory_reporter={"file_prefix": "opt_", "properties": ["potential_energy"]},
)

print(f"Energies: {result.energy.tolist()}")
print(f"Max forces: {ts.system_wise_max_force(result).tolist()}")
```

When `autobatcher=True`, the `optimize()` function automatically estimates the maximum memory your GPU can handle, then uses an `InFlightAutoBatcher` to swap converged states out and new states in. This means you can pass thousands of structures and the system will process them in memory-safe chunks without any manual configuration.

## Putting It All Together: Workflow Summary

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Prepare structures<br/>(ASE Atoms / Pymatgen)"] --> B{"Choose API level"}
    B -->|High-level| C["ts.optimize()<br/>Auto init, convergence,<br/>batching, reporting"]
    B -->|Low-level| D["_init() → loop {_step()}<br/>Manual control"]

    C --> E{"Cell relaxation?"}
    D --> E
    E -->|Yes| F["Pass cell_filter to<br/>init_kwargs or _init()"]
    E -->|No| G["Positions only"]
    F --> H["Run optimization"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["Extract results<br/>result.energy, result.positions"]
```

Sources: [runners.py](torch_sim/runners.py#L551-L730), [optimizers/__init__.py](torch_sim/optimizers/__init__.py#L1-L53)

- **[Automatic Batching and GPU Memory](18-automatic-batching-and-gpu-memory)** — How `BinningAutoBatcher` and `InFlightAutoBatcher` work under the hood, memory estimation, and custom batch size configuration.
- **[High-Level Runners API](19-high-level-runners-api)** — Complete reference for `integrate()`, `optimize()`, and `static()` runners including trajectory reporting and reproducible restarts.

# Architecture Overview



TorchSim is a PyTorch-native framework for atomistic simulation that unifies machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), molecular dynamics, geometry optimization, and Monte Carlo sampling under a single differentiable computation graph. Its architecture is organized around a **central state hierarchy** that flows through **pluggable model interfaces** into **modular simulation algorithms**, with **automatic batching** and **high-level runners** orchestrating the entire pipeline. This page maps out that architecture end-to-end, giving you the mental model needed to navigate the codebase and extend it for your own research.

## High-Level Architecture

The framework follows a layered architecture where each layer exposes both low-level primitives (for fine-grained control) and high-level runners (for rapid experimentation). Data flows downward from user-provided atomic structures through state initialization, model evaluation, and simulation algorithms, with optional batching and trajectory reporting wrapping the entire loop.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["Input Formats"]
        ASE["ASE Atoms"]
        PMG["Pymatgen Structures"]
        PH["PhonopyAtoms"]
        SS["SimState"]
    end

    subgraph Core["Core State System"]
        SIM["SimState"]
        MD["MDState"]
        OPT["OptimState"]
        FIRE["FireState"]
        BFGS["BFGSState / LBFGSState"]
        NPTMD["NPTLangevinState / NPTNoseHooverState"]
        MC["SwapMCState"]
        SIM --> MD
        SIM --> OPT
        OPT --> FIRE
        OPT --> BFGS
        MD --> NPTMD
        SIM --> MC
    end

    subgraph Models["Model Interface"]
        MI["ModelInterface<br/>(Abstract)"]
        MLIP["MLIP Models<br/>MACE, MACE-MP-0, SevenNet,<br/>ORB, FairChem, MatterSim"]
        CL["Classical Potentials<br/>LJ, Morse, Soft Sphere"]
        GPE["GraphPE Models"]
        MI --> MLIP
        MI --> CL
        MI --> GPE
    end

    subgraph Sim["Simulation Algorithms"]
        INT["Integrators<br/>NVE, NVT, NPT"]
        OPTZ["Optimizers<br/>FIRE, GD, L-BFGS, BFGS"]
        MCD["Monte Carlo<br/>Swap MC"]
    end

    subgraph Infra["Infrastructure"]
        NL["Neighbor Lists<br/>Vesin, Torch-NL, Linked Cell"]
        AB["Auto-Batching<br/>Binning / InFlight"]
        TR["Trajectory<br/>HDF5 Reporter"]
        CST["Constraints<br/>FixAtoms, FixCom, FixSymmetry"]
    end

    subgraph Runners["High-Level API"]
        INTG["integrate()"]
        OPTM["optimize()"]
        STAT["static()"]
    end

    Input --> Core
    Core --> Models
    Models --> Sim
    NL --> Models
    AB --> Runners
    CST --> Core
    Sim --> Runners
    TR --> Runners
    Runners --> INTG
    Runners --> OPTM
    Runners --> STAT
```

Sources: [torch_sim/__init__.py](/torch_sim/__init__.py#L104-L212), [torch_sim/runners.py](/torch_sim/runners.py#L252-L265)

## Package Structure

The `torch_sim/` package is divided into clearly delineated submodules, each responsible for a single concern. Understanding this layout is the first step toward navigating and contributing to the codebase effectively.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph torch_sim["torch_sim/"]
        direction TB
        state_py["state.py<br/>SimState hierarchy"]
        models_dir["models/<br/>ModelInterface + adapters"]
        integrators_dir["integrators/<br/>MD integrators"]
        optimizers_dir["optimizers/<br/>Geometry optimizers"]
        runners_py["runners.py<br/>integrate, optimize, static"]
        autobatching_py["autobatching.py<br/>GPU memory management"]
        neighbors_dir["neighbors/<br/>Vesin, Torch-NL"]
        transforms_py["transforms.py<br/>PBC & coordinate math"]
        constraints_py["constraints.py<br/>FixAtoms, FixCom, FixSymmetry"]
        trajectory_py["trajectory.py<br/>HDF5 I/O"]
        io_py["io.py<br/>ASE / Pymatgen / Phonopy bridges"]
        units_py["units.py<br/>Metal, Real unit systems"]
        elastic_py["elastic.py<br/>Elastic tensor calculation"]
        monte_carlo_py["monte_carlo.py<br/>Swap MC sampling"]
        properties_dir["properties/<br/>Correlation calculators"]
        workflows_dir["workflows/<br/>A2C crystallization"]
    end
```

| Module | Responsibility | Key Exports |
|--------|---------------|-------------|
| `state.py` | Core state dataclasses and manipulation | `SimState`, `concatenate_states`, `initialize_state` |
| `models/interface.py` | Abstract model contract | `ModelInterface` |
| `models/` | Concrete model adapters (13+ models) | `LennardJones`, `MaceModel`, `SevenNetModel`, etc. |
| `integrators/` | MD time-stepping algorithms | `nve_step`, `nvt_langevin_step`, `npt_nose_hoover_step`, etc. |
| `optimizers/` | Structure relaxation algorithms | `fire_step`, `lbfgs_step`, `bfgs_step`, `gradient_descent_step` |
| `runners.py` | High-level simulation loops | `integrate()`, `optimize()`, `static()` |
| `autobatching.py` | GPU memory-aware batch splitting | `BinningAutoBatcher`, `InFlightAutoBatcher` |
| `neighbors/` | Pair neighbor list construction | `torchsim_nl()` (auto-selecting best backend) |
